svg.text: Remote testing prerequisites
an account, credentials and permissions; create and populate streams and stores;
clean up afterwards (also on failure) without breaking others' tests; invest in
service accounts and permissions: it makes testing safer and also tests the
production permission configuration
Temporary single-tenant environment
created by IaC or a SaaS API, then discarded; exercises creating brokers each time;
crafted data lives in test code; mirror production partition counts so
copartitioning and repartitioning are tested; populate with production copies,
curated events, or generated events
From production
replicate streams, offsets or time ranges with the
replication tooling; accurate and isolated; costs:
production load (use quotas, throttle), big copies,
sensitive data, and no production keys to decrypt; good
for load tests against SLOs
Curated
service owners keep representative events (JSON, XML or
YAML) in the repo; others load them; validated on
parsing; may not exercise joins or aggregations, rots
like documentation, standards compete
Generated
built from schemas in the registry (Confluent Avro
tools, fuzzing for boundary data); you control values
and relationships (a join needs matching keys); an
early warning of schema drift; duplicated scripts,
stale, unlike production key skew; hybrid: curate core
entities, generate the rest
Durable multitenant environment: easy and isolated from production, but a tragedy of the commons (abandoned streams, polluted outputs, interfering load tests, stale
data) and the worst option for usability. Production testing: complete data and the real security model, good for smoke tests, but uses production resources, cannot do
load tests, needs cleanup and tooling to isolate (metadata tags help); write only to a temporary test stream. With little tooling you end up with a shared broker of
streams like -testing-02-final-v2; with tooling each service brings up, populates and tears down its own environment (non-trivial, but it also helps disaster recovery).
